text: A Ukrainian boarding school for the deaf runs a second curriculum, and Sergey is enrolled in it within days of arriving. Robbery, protection, a cut passed upward: a working business with ranks, conducted entirely in hands, wholly visible and closed to anyone who cannot read it. Slaboshpytskyi gives it 132 minutes, and the length is the method - rules get established by repetition, by who stands where in a corridor, by what happens to the boy who is slow handing money over. Ukraine later placed the film among the hundred best it has made. Then there is Anya, one of the Chief's women, and the part of the code nobody has written down turns out to be the part that gets enforced. Nothing here is explained to an outsider; the organisation is learned the way Sergey learns it, by watching what other people's faces do.

Joan Webster has the wedding scheduled, the clothes packed, and the crossing to the island timed to the minute; the weather has other arrangements. She is travelling to the Hebrides to marry a wealthy industrialist, and wind pins her on Mull among islanders unbothered by her itinerary and unimpressed by her certainty. It sits on TSPDT's list of the thousand greatest films, largely on the strength of what it does with a delay. Pressburger builds the comedy out of stalling - a boat that will not sail, a borrowed room, an evening nobody budgeted for - and keeps the money in plain view throughout, since the industrialist is rich at the start and stays rich. There is no villain here, only a naval officer named Torquil MacNeil, who belongs to the place in a way Joan does not and has not asked her to change anything.

Everything the film shows is being supplied by a woman who cannot see any of it. Ingrid lost her sight recently and has withdrawn into her flat, where she is safe, in control, and increasingly certain that her husband is at home during the hours he should be at work. There is a neighbour some distance away, and a woman he has begun to watch across the street, and how much of either exists outside Ingrid's head is never settled. Sundance gave Eskil Vogt's screenplay its world cinema prize, which is the right department: the film is a piece of construction, revising its own evidence as her fear moves. One apartment, Norwegian dialogue, and an account with a single source. The marriage at the centre is never argued about aloud; it is tested by what she chooses to picture, and she has no way to check.

A Lou Reed LP that came into Leningrad in somebody's luggage and went hand to hand until the sleeve softened is the kind of object this film treats as infrastructure. One summer in the early eighties, Perestroika still ahead of everyone, Mike and his wife Natasha meet a young Viktor Tsoi who has songs and no idea what they will be worth. The scene around them runs on imports and improvisation. Serebrennikov made the film in Russian on a French production, and its European Film Award went to the production designer - a fair reading of where the labour went, since a whole borrowed culture has to be built out of clothes, record sleeves and rooms. The songs keep arriving. It is not sentimental about scarcity; it watches what scarcity made people invent.

The sentence is community service, and the community turns out to be one policeman. Mariano, a psychologist, lost a lawsuit over a traffic accident, and his penalty is keeping Alfredo talking - a cop who has recently learned his wife is seeing someone else and who happens to be running a double homicide. Szifron writes the two of them into a single problem: neither man can end the appointment, one of them is armed, and the sessions do not stay in the office. At 112 minutes the murders keep their full weight, which is what stops the comedy going weightless - a joke about professional boundaries needs someone genuinely in danger of crossing one. What the case ends up demanding of Mariano is the thing his training forbids: opinions, advice, a side.

A student decides the world has been handed over to evil, and the adults around him turn out to have nothing prepared. Serebrennikov's film runs on that asymmetry. The boy is certain, and certainty is the one thing a school cannot issue a form for, so teachers, administrators and his own mother improvise their answers while he simply repeats his. The Russian setting works here in a plain institutional way - objections that would be a phase anywhere else land in staff meetings, where somebody has to minute them and reply. The European Film Award it took was for the score, which keeps his speeches pitched as a threat rather than a stage of growing up. Whether he is right is not the question the film is asking. How fast a room gives ground is.

Nobody has kept the house up in years, and now, his mother dead, it belongs to Yusuf. He has not been back in a long time; in the rooms is Ayla, a relative in her late teens whose existence he did not know of, who kept his mother company for five years and knows the town's routines the way he once did. He is a poet, which the film notes and then declines to turn into a personality. Kaplanoglu gives the situation almost no event - an obligation to see through, meals, roads, a bedside. The arithmetic underneath is impossible to argue with: somebody stayed, and it was not the son. What makes the film hold is that this is never said aloud. Ayla makes no claim, Yusuf offers no defence, and the house goes on needing repairs it needed long before he arrived.

The training camp is going badly for reasons no coach has a drill for. Summer 1962: Olli Mäki has a shot at the featherweight championship of the world, and Finland has arranged the rest - the trip from the countryside to Helsinki, the money, the photographs, the version of him that will be famous by autumn. His job is to make weight and concentrate. He has fallen in love with Raija instead, and Kuosmanen treats that as the actual event, with the title fight as the noise around it. The register stays small: people managing him, a schedule he did not write, a woman who was not in anybody's plan. The pleasure is watching a man be politely, completely unavailable to the largest week of his life, and better company than everyone arranging it.

Six men on a fishing trip in the Aegean decide to find out which of them is best - not at fishing, not at anything nameable, just best, in general, as men. So they keep score. Things are compared, things are measured, blood is sent off to be tested, a song is sung badly and marked down accordingly, and the winner will wear a ring on his little finger. Tsangari plays every bit of it at the temperature of a pleasant holiday, which is why it stays funny for a while: nobody proposes the game as a joke, and nobody asks to be excused. Greece sent the film to the Academy Awards. One yacht, no shore - the setting does the cruelty, since a man losing here cannot go home, take a walk, or find anyone who is not currently ranking him.

The monks in this film are monks: Rossellini cast the brothers of the Nocera Inferiore Monastery to play Francis and his companions. He wrote it with Federico Fellini and assembled it out of small self-contained episodes rather than a life with a rising line - humility, compassion, sacrifice, each told as an anecdote and then let go. Persuasion is not on the agenda; the episodes simply happen and stop. The images are composed after the paintings of the saint's own century, which gives the poverty a deliberate shape rather than a pitiable one, and the non-actors give the joy in it a plainness a trained cast would have ruined. TSPDT keeps the film among the thousand greatest. Whether that joy is available to someone who believes none of it is a question the film declines to raise.

In 1981 South Africa took two years of compulsory military service from its young men, and used them to make a particular kind of man. Oliver Hermanus follows one conscript through that training carrying something he cannot put down: he is gay, and the camp is arranged, hour by hour, to find exactly that out. The film is in Afrikaans, and the language is not decoration - it carries every order and every insult, and there is no hour of the day it does not reach. The racism is not a theme the film works toward; it is the declared content of the instruction. What Hermanus watches closest is small: how a young man trains his face to report nothing, holds it there for months, and learns what the practice has cost him when he is finally alone with someone.

Everybody in this small Dutch community wants something they will not be getting, and everybody knows what the neighbours want too. Alex van Warmerdam sets that in the 1960s and plays it flat: the obsessions are sexual, the manners are provincial, and the collision of the two is delivered in the tone of a weather report. The households sit side by side like sealed units, each with its private appetite, a street between them to carry the gossip. Nobody in the film treats any of this as scandalous - which is the joke, and also why it stings. What holds it together is the effort everyone spends keeping the surface intact while doing nothing of the kind underneath. A comedy that never once raises its voice, and never lets anybody off.

A fever makes an unreliable narrator, and this film hands it the job. Petrov draws comic books, has a family, and has caught whatever is going around; his friend Igor collects him and walks him through a day that will not stay in one register. Serebrennikov lets the illness do the editing, so scenes hand off without changing gears and a thing remembered arrives with the same weight as a thing happening. The film is filed as drama, comedy and science fiction at once, which is not a hedge but an inventory. Russian dialogue, French production, and 145 minutes that are clearly deliberate: sickness has no act structure and the film refuses to lend it one. What it is after is the texture of a bad week, in which the fantastic is one more errand to get through before evening.

A sea captain bets in a cafe that he will marry the next woman through the door, and then lives inside the consequence for a hundred and seventy minutes. Ildikó Enyedi takes an anecdote that would fill eight pages of a short story and runs it at the length of a marriage, which is the design rather than an accident: the joke is finished early, and what follows is the slow work of a man trying to know a person he acquired by wager. He is not a fool. He is someone used to being obeyed who has met a situation that does not answer to command, and who has no vocabulary for the difference. The Hungarian dialogue sits inside a French production. The running time is the argument - knowing another person is not an event, it is a practice, and practices need hours to show themselves.
